title: Is Subsequence
description: Brute force to optimized: recursive matching versus an iterative two pointer scan versus binary search for many queries.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given two strings s and t, return true if s is a subsequence of t, meaning every character of s appears in t in the same order, though not necessarily right next to each other.

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given two strings s and t, return true if s is a subsequence of t, meaning every character of s appears in t in the same order, though not necessarily right next to each other.

blocks.title: Analogy: Spelling a Word by Skipping Letters on a Sign
blocks.text: Like spelling out a short word by pointing at letters on a long storefront sign, moving only left to right and allowed to skip over any letters that are not needed, but never allowed to go backward.

blocks.caption: Every character of the shorter string must appear, in order, somewhere in the longer one

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: s = "abc", t = "ahbgdc"

blocks.text: Edge case: s is an empty string
An empty string requires nothing to be matched at all, so it is trivially a subsequence of any string, including another empty one, giving true.
5. How Should We Think?
It helps to ask whether the recursive structure of the brute force is really doing anything that a simple forward scan could not.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The recursive brute force correctly matches s against t one character at a time, but recursion adds call stack overhead for logic that only ever moves forward through both strings, never backward and never revisiting a position.

Observation 2: This is a same direction two pointer scan, distinct from the two pointers converging from opposite ends seen in Three Sum and Trapping Rain Water. Here, one pointer sweeps through t unconditionally while the other advances through s only when a match happens, so rewriting the recursion as a simple iterative loop changes nothing about the logic.

Observation 3: This single query approach is already optimal for checking one pair of strings, but a well known follow up asks whether the same long t needs to be checked against many different short query strings, and rescanning all of t for every single query wastes the fact that t itself never changes between queries.

Observation 4: Precomputing, once, a sorted list of positions for every letter in t turns each new query into a sequence of binary searches, jumping directly to the next valid occurrence of each needed letter after the previous match, confirmed by tracing s equal to "abc" against t equal to "ahbgdc" through both the two pointer scan and the binary search index to the identical answer, true.

Recognizing that this scan only ever moves forward is what allows the recursion to become a simple loop, and recognizing that t stays fixed across repeated queries is what justifies precomputing a position index once instead of rescanning t every time.
6. Brute Force Solution
Recursively try to match the first character of s somewhere in t, then recursively check whether the rest of s is a subsequence of whatever remains of t after that match.
Step by step algorithm

items: If s is empty, it is always a subsequence, return true.
If t is empty but s is not, return false.
If the first characters of s and t match, recurse on the rest of both strings.
Otherwise, recurse on all of s against the rest of t, skipping this character of t.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The two base cases, s exhausted or t exhausted, are checked first, since they immediately resolve the answer without any further comparison.
A matching pair of characters advances both pointers together, since that character of s has now been satisfied and should not be considered again.
A non matching pair only advances the pointer into t, since s must still wait for its current character to be found somewhere later.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every character of s is matched against t in order without ever going backward, so this correctly determines whether s is a subsequence.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m), where m is the length of t, since each recursive call advances the position in t by one.
Space: O(m), for the recursion call stack in the worst case, since no character of s ever matches.
Limitation: recursion adds call stack overhead and risks a stack overflow on very long strings, when the exact same logic can be expressed as a simple iterative loop instead.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: the recursion never revisits a position or moves backward, so its call stack overhead is pure cost with no benefit over a plain loop.

What an iterative two pointer scan fixes directly: the same forward only logic, expressed as a single loop over t with a second index into s, removes the recursion stack entirely.

What if this exact check needs to run many times against the same fixed t: rescanning all of t for every new query string wastes the fact that t's letter positions never change between queries.

The core idea: for a single query, a simple two pointer loop is already optimal; for many queries against the same t, precompute a sorted position list per letter once, then binary search within it for each query instead of rescanning t.

Replace the recursion with two simple pointers, one for s and one for t, both starting at the beginning. Walk the pointer through t one step at a time; whenever the characters at both pointers match, advance the s pointer as well. If the s pointer reaches the end of s, every character has been matched in order.
9. Optimized Solution
A single iterative pass with two pointers, advancing through t always, and through s only on a match.
Dry run for s = "abc", t = "ahbgdc"

blocks.caption: Optimized: two pointers, advancing through t always, and through s only on a match

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because advancing the s pointer only on a match guarantees every character of s is matched to a position in t strictly after the previous match, which is exactly the definition of appearing in order, and reaching the end of s proves every one of its characters was successfully located that way.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["The current character of t matches the character s is currently waiting for","The s pointer advances to look for the next character","One more character of s is confirmed to appear in the correct order"],["The s pointer reaches the end of s before t is fully scanned","The loop can stop early, or simply finish, since the answer is already determined","Every character of s has been matched, so the result is true"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m), a single pass through t.
Space: O(1), only the two pointers are kept, no recursion stack.
10. Further Optimization: Binary Search for Many Queries

If this check needs to be repeated for many different short strings against the same long string t, precompute, for every letter of the alphabet, a sorted list of every index in t where that letter appears. Then for each character of a query string s, instead of scanning forward through t, binary search within that letter's index list for the smallest position strictly after the previous match, jumping there directly. This turns each individual query into O(length of s times log of length of t) instead of O(length of t), which is a large win when there are many queries to answer against the same fixed t.
Dry run for t = "ahbgdc", query s = "abc"

blocks.caption: Further optimization: precomputed positions per letter, binary search for the next valid spot

codes.python:
from bisect import bisect_right
from collections import defaultdict

def build_index(t):
    positions = defaultdict(list)
    for idx, ch in enumerate(t):
        positions[ch].append(idx)                                # every index where this letter appears in t
    return positions

def is_subsequence_query(s, positions):
    last_match = -1
    for ch in s:
        candidates = positions.get(ch, [])
        idx = bisect_right(candidates, last_match)                  # first position strictly after the last match
        if idx == len(candidates):
            return False
        last_match = candidates[idx]
    return True


if __name__ == "__main__":
    t = "ahbgdc"
    s = "abc"
    index = build_index(t)
    print(is_subsequence_query(s, index))

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The index is built once, up front, storing every position where each letter occurs in t, in already sorted order since positions are appended as t is scanned left to right.
For each character needed by a query, binary search finds the first stored position strictly greater than the previous match, jumping directly there instead of scanning every character in between.
If no such position exists for a needed letter, the query fails immediately, since that letter cannot be found anywhere after the required point.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m) once to build the index, then O(length of s times log m) per query.
Space: O(m), for the precomputed position lists.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

The two pointer approach is already optimal for answering a single query, but this problem's well known follow up (many short strings checked against one long, fixed string) rewards precomputing structure once up front rather than rescanning the long string from scratch for every query.
Common Mistakes

items: Advancing the s pointer even when the characters do not match, which breaks the order requirement entirely.
Rebuilding the per letter position index for every single query when many queries share the same t, wasting the whole point of precomputing it once.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["An empty s","Always a subsequence."],["s longer than t","Can never be a subsequence and can be rejected immediately as a quick early exit."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Bring up the many queries follow up proactively, since it is the standard way this exact problem gets extended in interviews, and shows awareness of amortizing repeated work.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "what if you had to check this many times against the same t", think: precompute a sorted position list per letter, then binary search per query.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid recursion", think: the same forward only logic rewrites directly as an iterative two pointer loop.
If the interviewer says "what if s were longer than t", think: an immediate false, s cannot possibly be a subsequence of something shorter than itself.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why can the recursive solution be rewritten as an iterative loop with no change in logic?
Why does precomputing letter positions in t only help when there are many queries, not just one?
How would you find the length of the longest common subsequence instead of just checking one specific candidate?
How would this approach change if t itself could be modified between queries?
How would you check whether s is a subsequence of t if characters could also be case insensitive?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Three Sum and Trapping Rain Water, whose two pointers converge from opposite ends, a different shape from the same direction sweep used here.
Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array and Sqrt(x), whose binary search eliminates half a search space per step, the same tool reused here to jump to the next valid letter position.
Any "one long fixed reference checked against many short queries" problem, where precomputing a lookup structure once is almost always worth the upfront cost.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force (recursive): O(m) time, O(m) recursion stack space. Optimized (two pointers): O(m) time, O(1) space. Further optimized (many queries): O(m) time to build the index once, O(length of s times log m) per query after that.
13. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a same direction two pointer scan, further optimized with binary search over precomputed letter positions for repeated queries.

Core Idea: advance through t always, and through s only on a match, and every character of s reaching a match proves the whole string appears in order; for many queries against a fixed t, precompute letter positions once and binary search per query instead.
Time: O(m) for both the brute force and single query optimized versions, O(m) to build plus O(length of s times log m) per query for the further optimized version.
Space: O(m) recursion stack for the brute force, O(1) for the iterative version, O(m) for the precomputed index.
Most Important Observation: a forward only, never backward matching scan needs no recursion at all, and a fixed reference string checked repeatedly is worth indexing once.
Interview Difficulty: the single query solution is straightforward; proactively raising and solving the many queries follow up is what shows real depth.
One line memory trick: sweep t always, advance s only on a match; for many queries, binary search a precomputed position index instead.
